chapters.title: A Gathering Storm
beats: Across a contested landscape, sovereign nations prepare for an armed clash that will reshape regional boundaries in less than a week.
Israel stands opposed to a coalition of Arab neighbors, including Egypt, Jordan, and Syria, as longstanding border friction spirals into open mobilization.
The resulting confrontation displaces hundreds of thousands of people, establishes military occupations over vast lands, and permanently alters the geography of holy cities.
Decades later, the geopolitical consequences of those few contested days continue to define international diplomacy and territorial disputes.

chapters.title: Lines Drawn in the Sand
beats: The territories at stake—the Sinai Peninsula, the Gaza Strip, the West Bank, East Jerusalem, and the Golan Heights—form the strategic corridors and spiritual heartlands dividing Israel from its neighbors.
In Cairo, Gamal Abdel Nasser seeks regional leadership, rallying the Arab world against Israel while demanding the removal of peacekeepers from his borders.
In Damascus, Nureddin al-Atassi aligns Syria with Cairo through a mutual defense agreement, seeking to press Israel along their disputed northern frontier.
In Amman, King Hussein leads Jordan, initially accusing rival Arab leaders of hiding behind international peacekeepers before feeling compelled to join their joint military command.
In Jerusalem, Levi Eshkol leads an anxious Israeli government, bearing the dual weight of premier and defence minister while seeking to avoid premature escalation.
Alongside him, Yitzhak Rabin directs the military staff, preparing the army for a multi-front campaign if diplomatic avenues collapse.
chapters.hook: As pacts were signed and divisions converged on the frontiers, the countdown to an unavoidable choice began.

chapters.title: The Road to Mobilization
beats: In early November 1966, Nureddin al-Atassi concludes a mutual defense pact with Gamal Abdel Nasser, cementing an alliance between Syria and Egypt.
Tensions escalate after an April 1967 aerial clash downs six Syrian jets, followed by false Soviet intelligence reports warning Nasser that Israeli forces are concentrating along the Syrian frontier.
Nasser responds by mobilizing one hundred thousand troops into the Sinai Peninsula and expelling the United Nations Emergency Force from Gaza and Sinai.
Nasser escalates the standoff further by ordering the closure of the Straits of Tiran to Israeli shipping.
King Hussein flies to Cairo to sign a mutual defense pact with Nasser, after which Jordanian authorities invite Iraqi forces to deploy on Jordanian soil.
chapters.hook: With Arab armies united on three sides, Israeli leaders gathered behind closed doors to decide their nation's course.

chapters.title: The Decision in Jerusalem
beats: Faced with an imminent multi-front confrontation, Levi Eshkol widens his cabinet on 1 June 1967 to assemble an emergency National Unity Government.
Inside the cabinet room, Yitzhak Rabin and military planners report that the encircling armies present an existential hazard that cannot be deterred by diplomacy alone.
Eshkol hears the final arguments as ministers assess the grave diplomatic and human costs of striking first versus absorbing an opening blow.
On 4 June 1967, the Israeli cabinet formally casts its vote, authorizing the military to launch a preemptive campaign against the gathered forces.

chapters.title: Six Days of Fire
beats: On the morning of 5 June 1967, Israel launches Operation Focus, catching Egyptian airfields by surprise, destroying nearly all of Egypt's combat aircraft on the tarmac, and opening a rapid armored advance into the Sinai Peninsula and the Gaza Strip.
Later that morning, King Hussein commits Jordan to the fight by initiating an assault on West Jerusalem, broadening the war despite warnings to remain neutral.
By the morning of 6 June, Jordanian commanders conclude they cannot hold their defensive lines in the West Bank, while Egyptian commanders dispatch grim situation updates to Nasser.

On 7 June, Israeli forces secure the Old City of East Jerusalem, advance across the West Bank to take Hebron and surrounding areas, and establish military authority over the territory by issuing Proclamation Regarding Law and Administration (The West Bank Area) (No. 2)—1967.
Nasser orders a general retreat, allowing Israeli forces to fully occupy the Sinai Peninsula by 8 June, while Syria enters the conflict by shelling northern Israeli positions.

Israeli forces pivot northward, launching an assault against Syrian fortifications on the Golan Heights until fighting halts on 10 June, leaving Israel in control of Sinai, Gaza, the West Bank, East Jerusalem, and the Golan Heights.

chapters.title: A New Reality
beats: In the wake of the ceasefire, between 280,000 and 325,000 Palestinians flee or are expelled from the West Bank and Gaza Strip, while roughly 100,000 Syrians leave the Golan Heights.
On 19 June 1967, Levi Eshkol's National Unity Government votes unanimously to offer the return of the Sinai Peninsula to Egypt and the Golan Heights to Syria in exchange for formal peace treaties.
In August 1967, Arab heads of state assemble in Khartoum and reject negotiations, adopting a collective stance of no recognition, no peace, and no direct talks with Israel.
The United Nations Security Council adopts Resolution 242 in November 1967, articulating the land for peace formula to govern future regional settlements.
In 1978, Egypt and Israel sign the Camp David Accords, paving the way for a 1979 peace treaty that returns the Sinai Peninsula to Egypt while Gaza remains under Israeli control.
King Hussein concludes decades of hostility in 1994 by signing a bilateral peace treaty between Jordan and Israel, formalizing their shared boundary.
